Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s vision or eyes.
Parent: Our child has astigmatism, which makes it hard for him to see clearly. We're worried it might affect his schoolwork.

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child's hearing or ears.
Parent: He always turns the TV volume up really high. It's like he can't hear well unless it's blasting. I'm getting a bit concerned it could be a sign of a hearing problem.

Doctor: Please tell us about the problems with your child’s teeth.
Parent: We have to take him to the dentist a lot because his teeth are prone to problems. The dentist says he needs more frequent visits than average to keep them healthy.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s heart.
Parent: There's a structural issue with his heart that the doctors are monitoring. They say it's an abnormality that we should keep an eye on, but so far, it hasn't caused him any pain or discomfort.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child's hormones.
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about any neurological problem your child has (brain, nerves, muscle tone, fits).
Parent: He seems a bit clumsy compared to other kids. When he runs or plays, he often trips or stumbles. The doctors mentioned it could be related to coordination issues.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child's kidneys.
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s immune system (ability to fight infection and vaccination responses).
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child’s gastrointestinal system (feeding, stomach， bowel).
Parent: Constipation has been a real issue for our son. He struggles to go to the bathroom regularly and it causes him a lot of distress.

Doctor: Please use this box to tell us about any other medical problems that you haven’t been able to mention above.
Parent: He was born with shorter fingers than usual， which sometimes makes it tricky for him to hold onto things or do certain tasks that require finger dexterity.

# CLINICAL PATIENT REPORT

## 1) RESPIRATORY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 2) CARDIOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has a structural issue with his heart that requires monitoring.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 3) GASTROENTEROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient experiences constipation, which causes distress.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Feeding difficulties and lack of interest in feeding can be significant and long-lasting in some individuals with KBG syndrome.

## 4) IMMUNOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 5) NEUROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has clumsiness and trouble holding onto things due to a potential coordination issue.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, and some may have speech delay and subtle palate issues.

## 6) EAR NOSE THROAT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has a tendency to get otitis media or glue ear, which can lead to conductive hearing loss.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Many babies with KBG syndrome have feeding difficulties, and some require short-term nasogastric tube feeding to supplement oral feeds.

## 7) OPHTHALMOLOGY AND VISION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has astigmatism, making it hard for him to see clearly.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: People with KBG syndrome are more likely to have vision problems such as astigmatism and short- or long sightedness.

## 8) DERMATOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 9) DENTAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient needs to visit the dentist frequently due to tooth problems.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Dental concerns are common in KBG syndrome, including weak enamel and need for frequent check-ups and treatment.

## 10) EDUCATION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has difficulty in school due to various factors, including clumsiness and speech delay.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Children with KBG syndrome typically need extra help in school, though some go to mainstream primary school and others may require more support and may need to attend specialist settings.

## 11) BEHAVIOUR AND DEVELOPMENT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has clumsiness and trouble holding onto things due to a potential coordination issue, and also has speech delay.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, and some may have speech delay and subtle palate issues.

## 12) SKELETAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has an unusual structure of his spinal bones, which can give rise to an increased curvature of the spine.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Babies with KBG syndrome may experience delayed closure of the soft spot on their head, and some may have hip dysplasia, in which the hip joints are easily dislocated.

## 13) RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SCREENING AND TREATMENTS
a) Recommendations for screening: Regular dental check-ups, regular hearing reviews to age 5, eyesight (ophthalmology) review, check position of testes in boys, consider a palate review (particularly if there are feeding difficulties or speech concerns), consider a cardiac review following diagnosis, consider a skeletal review in children following diagnosis, consider review and investigation for tethered cord (MRI) where clinical concerns arise on an individual basis, monitor growth velocity: if height is below the 2nd centile consider referral for endocrine investigations on an individual basis and within context of familial heights.
b) Recommendations for treatments: Treatment options may include medication, physical therapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, and behavioral therapy. Monitoring and management plans should be tailored to the individual patient's needs and limitations. Regular monitoring of growth velocity and communication with healthcare providers are essential to ensure the best possible care.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s vision or eyes.
Parent: We've noticed he tends to sit very close to the TV when watching cartoons or leans in really close when looking at pictures in his books. It's almost as if he can't see them clearly from a normal distance.

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child's hearing or ears.
Parent: There are times when we call his name and he doesn't respond right away. It's not all the time, but often enough that we wonder if he's having trouble hearing us.

Doctor: Please tell us about the problems with your child’s teeth.
Parent: Lately, he's been complaing about tooth sensitivity when eating cold foods like ice cream or cold yogurt. This started a few months ago and has been consistent since then.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s heart.
Parent: The cardiologist found a structural abnormality in his heart. We go for regular check-ups to monitor it and make sure it doesn't affect his daily life too much.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child's hormones.
Parent: N/A

Doctor: Please tell us about any neurological problem your child has (brain, nerves, muscle tone, fits).
Parent: He was born with a tethered cord. The doctors said this could potentially affect his development and we're keeping a close eye on how he progresses.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child's kidneys.
Parent: N/A

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s immune system (ability to fight infection and vaccination responses).
Parent: N/A

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child’s gastrointestinal system (feeding, stomach, bowel).
Parent: Compared to his peers, our son gains weight slowly. He eats well and doesn't show signs of discomfort after eating but just doesn't seem to put on weight as quickly as other kids his age.

Doctor: Please use this box to tell us about any other medical problems that you haven’t been able to mention above.
Parent: Our child has scoliosis. We're working with physical therapy to help improve his posture and reduce the curvature of his spine.

b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, and some may have tethered cord, which means the spinal cord cannot move freely.

a) How this affects the patient: The patient experiences sensitive hearing when exposed to cold temperatures, such as ice cream or cold yogurt.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Feeding difficulties and subtle anomalies of the palate can affect speech development and feeding, and some individuals may require shorter-term tube feeding.

a) How this affects the patient: The patient has scoliosis, which affects his posture and reduces the curvature of his spine.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: People with KBG syndrome are more likely to have vision problems such as astigmatism and short- or long sightedness.

a) How this affects the patient: N/A

## 10) EDUCATION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has speech delay and takes longer to gain weight than his peers.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Children with KBG syndrome typically need extra help in school, and some may require Education Health Care Plans (EHCP).

## 11) BEHAVIOUR AND DEVELOPMENT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has developmental delay and various behavioral differences.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Approximately 50-70% of people with KBG syndrome have developmental delay, and some may have speech delay, subtle anomalies of the palate, and behavioral differences such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD), ADHD, or anxiety.

a) How this affects the patient: The patient has scoliosis, which affects his posture and reduces the curvature of his spine.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Individuals with KBG syndrome may have an unusual structure of their spinal bones, which can lead to an increased curvature of the spine (scoliosis).

a) How this affects the patient: The patient needs regular check-ups for his heart condition and has scoliosis.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: People with KBG syndrome may need periodic cardiology checks, surveillance for tethered cord, and monitoring for palatal abnormalities, especially if there are feeding difficulties or speech concerns.

# CLINICAL PATIENT REPORT

## 1) RESPIRATORY

b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 2) CARDIOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has a known structural abnormality in his heart that requires regular monitoring to ensure stability and control.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes, with some requiring surgery.

## 3) GASTROENTEROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient experienced significant challenges with feeding in infancy, including trouble latching on and getting frustrated during meal times, but these issues resolved over time.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Many babies with KBG syndrome have feeding difficulties, and some require short-term nasogastric tube feeding to supplement oral feeds.

## 4) IMMUNOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 5) NEUROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has developmental delay and is slower to reach certain milestones like walking or sitting compared to other children. Additionally, he has a noticeable difference in posture when standing or walking, which is being monitored by his healthcare team.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, and some may have tethered cord, which can cause pain and weakness in the legs, urinary and bowel issues, sacral dimple, and an unusual gait.

## 6) EAR NOSE THROAT
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Feeding difficulties and speech delay are common in KBG syndrome, with some individuals experiencing myopia and hypermetropia, as well as palatal abnormalities.

## 7) OPHTHALMOLOGY AND VISION
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: People with KBG syndrome are more likely to have vision problems such as astigmatism and short- or long sightedness, and squint can be a feature.

## 8) DERMATOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 9) DENTAL
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Dental concerns such as weak enamel and need for frequent tooth extractions or fillings are common in KBG syndrome.

## 10) EDUCATION
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Education-wise, most people with KBG syndrome enter puberty within the typical age range, but some may need more support and some benefit from specialist settings. Levels of educational attainment vary, with some children staying in mainstream education and obtaining qualifications, while others may require additional assistance.

## 11) BEHAVIOUR AND DEVELOPMENT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient experiences developmental delay and is slower to reach milestones, including walking and sitting.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Developmentally, people with KBG syndrome typically need extra help in school, though most children with the condition acquire mobility and other skills around the same age as “typical” children and some show more obvious delay.

## 12) SKELETAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has an unusual structure of his spinal bones, which can lead to an increased curvature of the spine (scoliosis), and delayed closure of the soft spot on his head (anterior fontanelle).
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: A proportion of people with KBG syndrome have an unusual structure of their spinal bones, which can give rise to an increased curvature of the spine (scoliosis).

## 13) RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SCREENING AND TREATMENTS
a) How this affects the patient: The patient needs regular monitoring for his heart condition, and has tethered cord, which may lead to complications such as sacral dimple and uneven gait.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Individuals with KBG syndrome may experience various neurological issues, including tethered cord, which could result in pain and weakness in the legs, urinary and bowel issues, sacral dimple, and an unusual gait. Monitoring and potential treatment options should be discussed with a specialist neurologist.
